section.title: The Stolen Blessing
section.sectionRationale: The promise of the older serving the younger, spoken before the twins were born, now collides with Isaac's plan to bless Esau. A family of four each pursues the blessing by scheming rather than trust, and the household is torn apart.
section.thesis: God's word that the older would serve the younger stands, yet the way it comes to pass exposes a family ruled by favoritism and deceit, so that even the right outcome is soaked in sin and grief.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: Isaac's plan for Esau; Rebekah and Jacob's deception; the trembling and Esau's lost blessing; and the murderous fallout that drives Jacob into exile.

units.label: Isaac plans to bless Esau
units.note: an old man and his favorite son

verses.text: When Isaac was old and his eyes were so weak that he could no longer see, he called his older son Esau and said to him, “My son.” “Here I am,” Esau replied.
“Look,” said Isaac, “I am now old, and I do not know the day of my death.
Take your weapons, your quiver and bow, and go out into the field to hunt some game for me.
Then prepare a tasty dish that I love and bring it to me to eat, so that I may {{barak|bless}} you before I die.”
Now Rebekah was listening to what Isaac told his son Esau. So when Esau went into the field to hunt game and bring it back,
Rebekah said to her son Jacob, “Behold, I overheard your father saying to your brother Esau,
‘Bring me some game and prepare me a tasty dish to eat, so that I may bless you in the presence of the LORD before I die.’
Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.
Go out to the flock and bring me two choice young goats, so that I can make them into a tasty dish for your father, the kind he loves.
Then take it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies.”
Jacob answered his mother Rebekah, “Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.
What if my father touches me? Then I would be revealed to him as a deceiver, and I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.”
His mother replied, “Your curse be on me, my son. Just obey my voice and go get them for me.”
So Jacob went and got two goats and brought them to his mother, who made the tasty food his father loved.
And Rebekah took the finest clothes in the house that belonged to her older son Esau, and she put them on her younger son Jacob.
She also put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
Then she handed her son Jacob the tasty food and bread she had made.
So Jacob went to his father and said, “My father.” “Here I am!” he answered. “Which one are you, my son?”
Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau, your {{bekor|firstborn}}. I have done as you told me. Please sit up and eat some of my game, so that you may bless me.”
But Isaac asked his son, “How did you ever find it so quickly, my son?” “Because the LORD your God brought it to me,” he replied.
Then Isaac said to Jacob, “Please come closer so I can touch you, my son. Are you really my son Esau, or not?”
So Jacob came close to his father Isaac, who touched him and said, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
Isaac did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like those of his brother Esau; so he blessed him.
Again he asked, “Are you really my son Esau?” And he replied, “I am.”
“Serve me,” said Isaac, “and let me eat some of my son’s game, so that I may bless you.” Jacob brought it to him, and he ate; then he brought him wine, and he drank.
Then his father Isaac said to him, “Please come near and kiss me, my son.”
So he came near and kissed him. When Isaac smelled his clothing, he blessed him and said: “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
May God give to you the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, an abundance of grain and new wine.

May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. May you be the master of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down to you. May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.”

units.label: Esau's lost blessing
units.note: the trembling and the bitter cry

verses.text: As soon as Isaac had finished blessing him and Jacob had left his father’s presence, his brother Esau returned from the hunt.
He too made some tasty food, brought it to his father, and said to him, “My father, sit up and eat of your son’s game, so that you may bless me.”
But his father Isaac replied, “Who are you?” “I am Esau, your firstborn son,” he answered.
Isaac began to tremble violently and said, “Who was it, then, who hunted the game and brought it to me? Before you came in, I ate it all and blessed him, and indeed, he will be blessed!”
When Esau heard his father’s words, he let out a loud and bitter cry and said to his father, “Bless me too, O my father!”
But Isaac replied, “Your brother came {{mirmah|deceitfully}} and took your blessing.”

So Esau declared, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me twice. He took my {{bekorah|birthright}}, and now he has taken my blessing.” Then he asked, “Haven’t you saved a blessing for me?”
But Isaac answered Esau: “Look, I have made him your master and given him all his relatives as servants; I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What is left that I can do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” Then Esau wept aloud.
His father Isaac answered him: “Behold, your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above.
You shall live by the sword and serve your brother. But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.”
Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. And Esau said in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.”
When the words of her older son Esau were relayed to Rebekah, she sent for her younger son Jacob and told him, “Look, your brother Esau is consoling himself by plotting to kill you.
So now, my son, obey my voice and flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides,
until your brother’s rage against you wanes and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I lose both of you in one day?”
Then Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women. If Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them, what good is my life?”

barak.gloss: To bless, to speak good and empowered life over someone. In the patriarchal narratives the spoken blessing carries the covenant promises of Abraham forward to the next generation. Isaac means to lay this weighty word on Esau, but it lands on Jacob instead.

bekor.gloss: The firstborn son, who normally held the place of honor and the larger inheritance. Jacob claims this title with his lie, 'I am Esau, your firstborn.' The whole story turns on the reversal of the firstborn's expected privilege.

mirmah.gloss: Deceit, treachery, a lie dressed up to look true. Isaac says Jacob came with mirmah and took the blessing. The same deceitful son will himself be deceived by Laban, and later by his own sons over Joseph.

bekorah.gloss: The birthright, the firstborn's double portion and headship of the family. Esau had earlier despised and sold his bekorah for a bowl of stew. Now he grieves that Jacob has taken both birthright and blessing.

basic.context: Isaac is old and blind and wants to bless his favorite son Esau before he dies. Rebekah, who favors Jacob, overhears and hatches a plan to steal the blessing by dressing Jacob as his brother. The key question is how God's earlier word, that the older would serve the younger, relates to this tangle of favoritism and lies.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a description of what happened, not a model to copy. Every person in the chapter sins: Isaac ignores God's word, Esau despises his birthright, Rebekah schemes, Jacob lies to his father's face. Yet God's purpose that the younger would carry the promise still comes to pass through it all.
basic.originalLanguages: The blessing, barak, is a weighty spoken word that hands on the promises of Abraham. Jacob lies that he is the bekor, the firstborn. Isaac later says he came with mirmah, deceit. Esau grieves that Jacob has taken both his bekorah, birthright, and his blessing.
basic.typology: The blessing that comes to the younger and unlikely son, not the expected firstborn, fits a pattern God repeats through Scripture and fulfills in Christ, who becomes the true firstborn and inheritor. Jacob receives a blessing he does not deserve, a faint pointer to grace given to the undeserving.
basic.christ: God works His good purpose even through a family's sin, the pattern that reaches its height at the cross, where wicked hands carry out God's plan of salvation. The blessing of Abraham, wrongly grasped here, finally flows to the nations through Christ, the true seed.
basic.god: God is sovereign: His word that the older would serve the younger stands, and no scheme can overturn it. Yet He is not the author of the sin; the deceit is real and brings real grief. God's faithfulness to His promise is not the same as approval of the way people pursue it.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 9 cites this family to show God's election rests on His call, not human merit. Hebrews 11 and 12 look back on both Isaac's faith and Esau's regret. Galatians 3 says the blessing of Abraham comes to the nations in Christ.
basic.oneStory: The covenant promise passes to Jacob, the man who will become Israel. But the ugly means expose why this family, and every family, needs a Savior. The blessing they fight over so sinfully will one day be secured and shared freely by the Son who obeys where they deceive.

context.literary:
Genesis 27 is staged as a sequence of two person scenes, and the characters are never all in the room together. Isaac speaks with Esau, verses 1 to 4; Rebekah with Jacob, verses 5 to 17; Isaac with Jacob, verses 18 to 29; Isaac with Esau, verses 30 to 40; Rebekah with Jacob again, verses 42 to 45; and finally Rebekah with Isaac, verse 46. The staging itself tells the story of a family that no longer talks to one another. Each person acts on information the others do not have, and the whole plot runs on things overheard.

The centre of the chapter is the long scene between Isaac and Jacob, built around the father's senses. His eyes have failed, verse 1, so he tests with touch, verse 21, weighs the voice against the hands, verse 22, tastes the food and wine, verse 25, and finally smells the clothing, verse 27. Each sense is deceived except hearing, and hearing is overruled.

Key words knit the chapter together. 'Bless' and 'blessing' dominate, appearing in almost every scene. 'Tasty dish' or 'tasty food' appears six times, in verses 4, 7, 9, 14, 17 and 31, keeping Isaac's appetite in view, as it was in Genesis 25:28. 'Voice' recurs as well: Rebekah tells Jacob 'listen to my voice' and 'obey my voice' in verses 8, 13 and 43, and Isaac says, 'The voice is the voice of Jacob.' The phrase recalls Genesis 3:17, 'you have listened to the voice of your wife,' and Genesis 16:2, where Abram 'listened to the voice of Sarai.' The contrast with Abraham, who 'obeyed My voice,' Genesis 22:18, is pointed.

The chapter mirrors Genesis 25. There Esau came in from the field and traded his birthright for food; here Esau goes out to the field for food and loses his blessing. He himself links the two losses in verse 36. The ending looks ahead. Jacob's deception with a goat and a brother's clothing will be answered when his own sons deceive him with a goat and a brother's robe, Genesis 37:31-33.
context.historical:
A father's final blessing was a formal and weighty act. It was spoken aloud, often in connection with a meal, and it was understood to shape the future of the one who received it. Genesis records several such scenes: Isaac here and in Genesis 28:1-4, Jacob blessing Joseph's sons and then all his sons in Genesis 48 and 49, and Moses blessing the tribes in Deuteronomy 33. Hebrews 11:20-21 treats both Isaac's and Jacob's blessings as acts of faith concerning the future.

Isaac speaks as a man about to die, 'I do not know the day of my death,' verse 2, and Esau plans to wait for 'the days of mourning for my father,' verse 41. Yet Isaac lives on for many years; Genesis 35:28-29 records his death at 180, with Esau and Jacob together at the burial. The deathbed atmosphere is Isaac's sense of things, not the end of his story.

The disguise depends on details of pastoral life. Goat hair was coarse and dark and could imitate a hairy man's arms. The goats come from the family's own flock, the flock Jacob kept as the man who stayed among the tents. Esau's 'finest clothes,' verse 15, were kept in the house, and they carried the smell of the open country Isaac loved.

The content of the blessing reflects the hopes of a farming and herding people: dew, which in the dry summer of Canaan kept crops alive, 'the richness of the earth,' grain and new wine. Deuteronomy 33:28 gathers the same images for Israel's future, 'a land of grain and new wine, where even the heavens drip with dew.' Rebekah's closing concern about 'these Hittite women' picks up Genesis 26:34-35 and the family's refusal to marry into the peoples of Canaan, Genesis 24:3-4.
context.canonical:
The blessing on Jacob sounds like the promise to Abraham turned into a royal oracle. 'May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed' takes up Genesis 12:3, and Balaam later repeats it over Israel, Numbers 24:9. 'May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you' is language of kingship. Jacob will pass it on to Judah, 'your father's sons shall bow down to you,' Genesis 49:8, and Psalm 72:11 prays for the king, 'May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.'

The oracle to Esau, that he would serve his brother and then break his yoke, is traced in Israel's history. David subdued Edom, 2 Samuel 8:14, and Edom rebelled in the days of Jehoram, 2 Kings 8:20-22 and 2 Chronicles 21:8-10.

The theme of deceit reappears through Genesis. Laban deceives Jacob by substituting the older daughter for the younger, 'It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older,' Genesis 29:26, a rebuke Jacob can hardly miss. Jacob's sons deal 'deceitfully' with Shechem, Genesis 34:13, and deceive their father over Joseph, Genesis 37:31-33.

The New Testament looks at the chapter three times. Hebrews 11:20 says, 'By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future,' treating Isaac's words as faith in God's purpose despite everything. Hebrews 12:17 recalls Esau who 'sought the blessing with tears' and was rejected. Romans 9:10-13 grounds Jacob's standing not in his conduct in this chapter but in God's choice before birth. And Galatians 3:14 names what was really at stake: 'the blessing promised to Abraham,' which comes 'to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know that their very name, Jacob, carried a mixed inheritance. They were the heirs of a real blessing spoken by their father Isaac, and they were descended from a man who got it by lying. The chapter refuses to flatter Israel's ancestor. It shows that the nation's privileges came by God's word, not by the virtue of the one who received them.

The author also meant Israel to see that God's word cannot be manipulated or overturned. Isaac tried to bless the son he preferred and found himself blessing the son God had chosen. Rebekah and Jacob tried to secure God's promise by their own methods and found that it came at a terrible cost. The purpose of God stood, as Proverbs 19:21 puts it: 'Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.'

Finally, the chapter teaches that sin has consequences even when God's purpose is fulfilled. The family is broken, Jacob is exiled, Rebekah loses her favourite son, and Esau becomes the father of a people with a long grudge. Israel was meant to learn that the ends do not sanctify the means, and that the blessing is best received from God's hand, not seized.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
No one in the chapter is held up as a model. Isaac tries to bless Esau privately, apparently setting aside the oracle of Genesis 25:23. Rebekah plans the deception and takes the curse on herself. Jacob lies three times, 'I am Esau, your firstborn,' 'the LORD your God brought it to me,' and 'I am,' invoking God's name in the middle of a lie. Esau plans murder. The narrator records all of it without approval.

The principle the New Testament draws is plain: we may not 'do evil that good may result,' Romans 3:8. Knowing God's purpose does not license us to pursue it by sin. What is commended, by Hebrews 11:20, is Isaac's final faith, in which he accepts the outcome, 'and indeed, he will be blessed!', and later blesses Jacob knowingly, Genesis 28:3-4. Believers are also warned by the example of Esau, Hebrews 12:17, and by the reaping of Jacob, since 'whatever a man sows, he will reap in return,' Galatians 6:7.

debates.question: Was Jacob's deception approved by God because it fulfilled the oracle?

views.label: God used it but did not approve it
views.case: The text shows Jacob reaping what he sowed. He is deceived by Laban with an older sister in place of a younger, Genesis 29:25-26, and by his own sons with a goat and a garment, Genesis 37:31-33. Twenty years of exile follow, Genesis 31:41. The consequences mark the sin as sin, even as God's purpose advances.

views.label: Rebekah acted on the oracle, but by the wrong means
views.case: Rebekah alone had received the word that the older would serve the younger, Genesis 25:23, and she may have believed she was preventing Isaac from overturning it. On this view her aim was right and her method wrong, a failure to trust God to fulfil His word His way, like Sarai offering Hagar in Genesis 16:2.

views.label: The ends justified the means
views.case: Some have argued that since God had promised the blessing to Jacob, Rebekah and Jacob were merely securing what God had decreed. The narrative gives little support for this: Jacob fears a curse, verse 12, and the rest of the story is full of the grief the scheme caused.

debates.bearing: Paul rules out the third view directly, Romans 3:8. The first two together fit the text: God's word was never in danger, and the family's scheming added nothing to it but pain.

debates.question: Why could Isaac not take the blessing back?

views.label: Spoken blessings were thought to be irreversible
views.case: In the ancient world a solemn blessing was often regarded as a word with power of its own, once released, not to be recalled. On this view Isaac's 'he will be blessed' reflects the cultural weight of the spoken word.

views.label: Isaac recognised God's hand
views.case: Isaac 'began to tremble violently,' verse 33, a reaction larger than mere shock at a trick. He seems to realise that God had overruled his own intention. Hebrews 11:20 calls his blessing an act of faith, and in Genesis 28:3-4 Isaac knowingly passes 'the blessing of Abraham' to Jacob. Balaam's confession offers a parallel: 'He has blessed, and I cannot change it,' Numbers 23:20.

debates.bearing: The second reading fits the wider story. The blessing held not because words are magic but because God had spoken first, and Isaac, at last, bowed to that.

debates.question: In Hebrews 12:17, whose 'repentance' could Esau not find?

views.label: Isaac's change of mind
views.case: Esau sought a reversal of his father's decision. The 'repentance' in view is a change in the situation, Isaac's willingness to revoke the blessing, which Genesis 27:33-37 shows could not happen.

views.label: Esau's own repentance
views.case: Others read the verse as a warning that Esau's tears were for the lost blessing, not for his contempt of God. He wanted the benefit without a changed heart, and his next thought was murder, Genesis 27:41.

debates.bearing: Either way the warning in Hebrews is the same. There comes a point where the consequences of despising God's gift cannot be undone by tears, so the call is to treasure grace now, Hebrews 12:15-16.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter is full of carefully chosen words beyond barak and bekor. The first is hinneni, 'Here I am.' Esau answers his father with it in verse 1, and Isaac answers Jacob with it in verse 18. It is the word Abraham spoke to God on Moriah, Genesis 22:1, and to Isaac himself on the way up the mountain, Genesis 22:7. The word of readiness that once marked trust now opens a chapter of deception.

The verb nagash, 'to come near,' runs through the central scene. Isaac says, 'Please come closer so I can touch you,' verse 21; Jacob 'came close,' verse 22; Isaac says, 'Please come near and kiss me,' verse 26; and 'he came near and kissed him,' verse 27. Each approach brings Jacob closer to the blessing and deeper into the lie. The approach of the son to the father, which should be the most natural thing in the world, has become a performance.

The word play around Esau's body continues from chapter 25. Jacob says, 'my brother Esau is a hairy man,' ish sa'ir, verse 11. The adjective sa'ir, 'hairy,' is also the common word for a male goat. So Jacob disguises himself as his hairy brother with the skins of goats. When his sons later deceive him, they slaughter 'a young goat,' se'ir izzim, and dip Joseph's robe in its blood, Genesis 37:31. The same animal serves both deceptions.

The verb 'recognize,' nakar, also links the two. Isaac 'did not recognize him,' verse 23. In Genesis 37:32-33 the brothers say, 'Examine it,' literally 'recognize, please,' and Jacob 'recognized it.' In Genesis 38:25-26 Tamar says to Judah, 'Please examine them,' and he 'recognized the items.' The same root marks the family's cycle of deceit and exposure.

Isaac's reaction in verse 33 is described with a doubled construction, literally 'Isaac trembled a great trembling, exceedingly.' Esau's response in verse 34 is built the same way: he 'cried out a great and bitter cry, exceedingly,' the loud and bitter wail of grief also used of Mordecai in Esther 4:1. The narrator matches father and son in the intensity of their distress.

The word Isaac uses in verse 35, mirmah, 'deceit,' comes from a root that returns when Jacob confronts Laban: 'Why have you deceived me?' Genesis 29:25. It appears again when Jacob's sons answer Shechem 'deceitfully,' Genesis 34:13. The deceiver is deceived, and then his sons carry the trait forward.

Esau's lament in verse 36 turns on sound. He took my bekorah, 'birthright,' and now my berakah, 'blessing,' two words that differ only by the order of their consonants. The same verse makes the pun on Jacob's name explicit. 'He has cheated me' is ya'qeveni, 'he has Jacobed me,' as the BSB footnote hints, 'he grasps the heel or he deceives.'

Finally, Isaac's words to Esau in verse 39 reuse the words of Jacob's blessing with a single change of sense. In verse 28 Jacob receives 'of the dew of heaven' and 'of the richness of the earth,' using the Hebrew preposition min in its sense 'some of.' In verse 39 the same preposition is attached to the same nouns, but now in its sense 'away from.' The BSB translates it, 'away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above.' One tiny word turns a blessing into its shadow.

typology.type: The younger son clothed in his brother's garments
typology.fulfillment: Jacob comes to his father wearing the clothes of the firstborn and receives the blessing because he smells like the brother his father loves. Some early Christian writers saw here a picture of believers coming to God clothed in Christ. Scripture supplies the reality: 'all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ,' Galatians 3:27, and 'He has clothed me with garments of salvation,' Isaiah 61:10. The type breaks down sharply at the point of truth. Jacob's clothing was a lie and stolen; Christ's righteousness is true and freely given, and God is not deceived but gracious. The contrast is part of the lesson.

typology.type: The blessing of Abraham coming to the undeserving
typology.fulfillment: Jacob receives a blessing he did not deserve and could not earn by his scheme. Paul says Christ redeemed us 'in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus,' Galatians 3:14, and that God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3. The escalation is that Jacob's blessing concerned grain, wine and rule over his brothers, while the blessing in Christ is the gift of the Spirit and an eternal inheritance, Ephesians 1:13-14. Unlike Jacob, believers do not have to steal it; it is offered freely.

typology.type: 'May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you'
typology.fulfillment: Isaac's blessing gives Jacob a royal destiny that Jacob himself never enjoyed; he bowed seven times to Esau, Genesis 33:3. The promise narrows to Judah, Genesis 49:8-10, rises in the prayer for the king, Psalm 72:11, and finds its fulfilment in Christ, at whose name 'every knee should bow,' Philippians 2:10. The type falls short because Jacob's line ruled by conquest and Edom broke its yoke. Christ's kingdom comes by His servanthood and cross, and His rule is everlasting.

typology.type: 'Your curse be on me, my son'
typology.fulfillment: Rebekah offers to take on herself the curse her son might incur, verse 13. This is a type by contrast. Her words were rash, and she paid for them by losing Jacob, apparently never to see him again. Christ really did take a curse that belonged to others: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, and 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Rebekah took a curse to secure a blessing by deceit; Christ took the curse to secure blessing by truth and self-giving.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by showing how badly the heirs of the promise need Him. Everyone in this family wants the blessing, and everyone reaches for it wrongly. Isaac wants to give it on the basis of appetite, Esau wants it without the birthright he sold, Rebekah and Jacob want it by deceit. The blessing of Abraham is real, but the family carrying it cannot carry it well. The chapter leaves the reader waiting for an heir who will receive the Father's blessing without deceit and share it without grasping.

It leads to Christ as that true Son. Jacob came to his father pretending to be someone else and lied three times to his face. Jesus could say, 'the Father loves the Son,' John 5:20, and He came to the Father as Himself, the beloved Son in whom the Father was well pleased. Jacob invoked 'the LORD your God' to cover a lie; Jesus is the truth, and 'no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22.

It leads to Christ through the garments. Jacob obtained his father's blessing by wearing his brother's clothes. The gospel reverses the moral logic while keeping the picture: believers come before the Father clothed with Christ, Galatians 3:27, not as a trick but as a gift. The Father is not deceived; He sees exactly who we are and gives us the robe anyway, like the father in the parable who calls for 'the best robe,' Luke 15:22.

It leads to Christ through the blessing itself. The words of verse 29 point beyond Jacob, who never saw nations bow to him. They pass through Judah, Genesis 49:10, and the royal psalms, and they rest on the Son of David, to whom 'every knee should bow,' Philippians 2:10. The promise that those who bless him will be blessed and those who curse him will be cursed becomes the dividing line of the gospel, since people are blessed or cursed by how they respond to Christ.

It leads to Christ through the curse. Rebekah said, 'Your curse be on me.' Christ actually bore the curse, Galatians 3:13, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations. He did it not by deceit but by self-offering, not to win a blessing for Himself but to give it away.

Finally, the chapter leads to Christ as the answer to Esau's cry. 'Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too!' In the gospel the Father's blessing is not limited to one son. In Christ, Jews and Gentiles, younger and older alike, can receive 'every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3. Esau's tears came too late because he despised what was offered. The gospel invites those who hear it not to wait, but to receive the blessing now.
study.god:
The chapter shows God chiefly by His hiddenness. He is never described as acting, and He does not speak. The covenant name appears only three times: a mother adds it to her husband's words, 'in the presence of the LORD,' verse 7, a son uses it to cover a lie, verse 20, and a father uses it in blessing, verse 27. Yet the reader knows from Genesis 25:23 that God has already spoken, and the chapter shows His word coming true through people who are not listening to Him. This is the God of providence, who rules without always appearing.

He is sovereign over human plans. Isaac planned to bless Esau, Rebekah planned to redirect the blessing, Esau planned revenge. None of them achieves what they wanted. Isaac blesses the wrong son, Rebekah loses the son she loved, Esau never kills Jacob, and the meeting of Genesis 33 ends in an embrace. Proverbs 16:9 states the principle: 'A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps.'

He is faithful to His word despite His people's faithlessness. The oracle of Genesis 25:23 is fulfilled, not because anyone trusted it, but because God does not lie. Balaam would later say, 'God is not a man, that He should lie,' Numbers 23:19. Paul uses this very family to show that God's purpose stands by His call, Romans 9:11.

He is holy, and He does not approve sin because He uses it. Scripture never holds God responsible for the lies of this chapter, and it shows Him disciplining the liar. The later chapters are the proof: Jacob is deceived by Laban and then by his sons. God can weave evil into His purposes, as Joseph says, 'what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good,' Genesis 50:20, but the evil remains evil, and those who do it answer for it.

He is gracious to the undeserving. Jacob received the blessing without deserving it. Even Esau is not left with nothing; he receives a word about his future, and God later gives his descendants their own land, Deuteronomy 2:5. Hebrews says Isaac blessed both sons 'by faith,' Hebrews 11:20.

This chapter holds a tension that runs through the whole Bible. God's purpose is certain, and human choices are real. The cross is its sharpest form: Jesus was delivered up 'by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' and those who crucified Him did so 'by the hands of the lawless,' Acts 2:23. For worship, the chapter calls us to trust God's word enough not to manipulate it. We do not have to scheme for God's blessing. We can receive it, as Isaac finally did, by faith.

crossReferences.note: The oracle given to Rebekah before the twins' birth, 'the older will serve the younger,' is the key to Genesis 27. Isaac's plan runs against it, Rebekah's scheme tries to secure it, and the outcome fulfils it. The chapter shows God's word standing while the family ignores or mishandles it.

Laban deceives Jacob by giving him Leah instead of Rachel, and answers, 'It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.' Jacob, who disguised the younger as the older, is now fooled in the dark with the older in place of the younger.

Jacob's sons slaughter a young goat, dip Joseph's robe in the blood, and ask their father to 'examine' it. Jacob, who once used goat skins and his brother's clothes to deceive a blind father, is himself deceived by goat's blood and a son's clothing.

Isaac now blesses Jacob knowingly and passes on 'the blessing of Abraham,' land and descendants, under the name God Almighty. The blessing obtained by deceit in Genesis 27 is confirmed openly, showing that Isaac has accepted God's choice.

'By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning the future.' Despite the confusion of Genesis 27, Hebrews sees faith in Isaac's words. He spoke about a future that belonged to God, and when he understood what had happened, he let God's word stand.

Esau 'sought the blessing with tears' and was rejected, finding 'no ground for repentance.' Hebrews connects the lost blessing of Genesis 27 with the birthright sold in Genesis 25, and uses both as a warning against treating grace lightly.

Christ became a curse for us so that 'the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus.' The blessing Jacob seized in Genesis 27 is the same blessing of Abraham, and Paul shows where it finally lands: on all who believe, through the One who bore the curse.

Isaac's words 'May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed' repeat the promise God made to Abraham. The patriarchal blessing is God's own covenant promise passed down, not merely a father's wish.

Twenty years later Jacob bows seven times to Esau, and Esau runs to embrace him. The blessing said that Jacob's mother's sons would bow to him, but the first bowing in the reunion is Jacob's own. The murderous grudge of Genesis 27:41 dissolves in tears.

In the days of Jehoram, 'Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king.' Isaac's word to Esau, 'when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck,' Genesis 27:40, is traced into the history of the kingdom.

'Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.' The proverb could stand as the title of Genesis 27, where four people plan and scheme, and God's purpose announced in Genesis 25:23 prevails.

Paul rejects the idea 'Let us do evil that good may result.' Rebekah and Jacob acted as if God's good purpose justified their deceit. Paul's principle shows that God's purposes never excuse sin committed in their name.

study.oneStory:
The blessing at stake in Genesis 27 goes back to the very beginning. God blessed the first humans in Genesis 1:28, and after the fall He began to restore that blessing through Abraham: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. Isaac's words to Jacob pass on that promise. So the question of this chapter is not only which twin gets his father's inheritance, but through whom God's plan to bless the world will run.

It answers what came before. The oracle of Genesis 25:23 said the older would serve the younger, and here it comes to pass. But the chapter also shows the fall at work inside the chosen family. As Adam listened to the voice of his wife, Jacob listens to his mother's voice. As the first brothers ended in murder, Esau plans to kill Jacob. The blessing is moving forward, but the curse is not yet broken.

It sets up what follows. Jacob flees and meets God at Bethel in Genesis 28, spends twenty years under a deceiver, and wrestles with God at Peniel, where he receives a new name, Israel, Genesis 32:28. The deceit of this chapter echoes through the next generation, in Joseph's robe and a goat's blood. The blessing's royal language passes to Judah, and Israel's long history with Edom begins in Esau's grudge.

The story comes to its centre in Christ. He is the true Son who receives the Father's blessing without deceit, the King before whom nations bow, the One who bore the curse Rebekah rashly offered to carry. Through Him the blessing of Abraham reaches the nations, Galatians 3:14, and there is more than one blessing to go around, for all who are in Him.

The new creation completes it. Every tear Esau shed and every grief this family caused will be answered when God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4. Deceit will have no place, for nothing false will enter the city of God, and those who come will be clothed not in borrowed garments but in the fine linen God gives, Revelation 19:8. Jesus will say to them, 'Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom,' Matthew 25:34. The blessing that one family fought over will be given freely to a multitude from every nation.

quiz.q: What did Rebekah and Jacob do to secure Isaac's blessing?

options.text: They disguised Jacob as Esau and lied to the blind Isaac to steal the blessing.
options.note: The plan turned on deception: goat skins, Esau's clothes, and an outright lie.

options.text: They prepared food Isaac loved and asked him to bless Jacob honestly.
options.note: The food was real, but the whole point was to deceive Isaac about who he was blessing.

options.text: They reminded Isaac of God's word that the older would serve the younger.
options.note: They never appeal to the oracle; they scheme instead of trusting it.

options.text: They forced Isaac to bless Jacob against his will.
options.note: Isaac was deceived, not coerced; he blessed Jacob believing he was Esau.

quiz.q: How does God's earlier word to Rebekah relate to this chapter?

options.text: God had said the older would serve the younger, and that purpose stands despite the sin.
options.note: The oracle of Genesis 25:23 is fulfilled, though not by means God commends.

options.text: God's word is fulfilled, which shows the deception was therefore good.
options.note: The purpose is fulfilled, but the text treats the deceit as real sin with real consequences.

options.text: God's word failed because Isaac tried to bless Esau.
options.note: God's word does not fail; the blessing lands on Jacob after all.

options.text: God had said nothing about the two sons beforehand.
options.note: God had spoken clearly before their birth that the older would serve the younger.

quiz.q: How should we understand every character's part in the story?

options.text: Each one sins: Isaac's favoritism, Esau's past contempt, Rebekah's scheme, Jacob's lie.
options.note: The narrative exposes a whole family ruled by favoritism and deceit.

options.text: Jacob alone is at fault for lying to his father.
options.note: Jacob does lie, but the sin is shared across the family.

options.text: Only Esau is to blame for losing what he had already despised.
options.note: Esau bears real guilt, but he is not the only sinner here.

options.text: No one really does wrong; it is just how blessings worked back then.
options.note: The chapter clearly frames deception and favoritism as sin, not custom.

quiz.q: What happens to Jacob as a result of the stolen blessing?

options.text: Esau vows to kill him, and Jacob must flee into years of exile with Laban.
options.note: The blessing he grasped costs him home, mother, and safety; he reaps what he sowed.

options.text: He enjoys the blessing at home in peace.
options.note: He gains the blessing but immediately loses his home and must flee for his life.

options.text: Isaac takes the blessing back and gives it to Esau.
options.note: Isaac says the blessing stands; it cannot be revoked.

options.text: Nothing changes; the family carries on as before.
options.note: The family is fractured, and Jacob is driven away in fear.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point us toward Christ?

options.text: God advances His saving purpose even through sinful means, as He does supremely at the cross.
options.note: The blessing of Abraham, grasped here by deceit, is finally secured righteously in Christ.

options.text: It shows that clever planning is how God's promises come true.
options.note: God's purpose stands, but the chapter warns against scheming, not commends it.

options.text: It teaches that the firstborn always deserves the blessing.
options.note: The story overturns natural precedence; the younger receives the promise.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ or the wider story.
options.note: The blessing of Abraham runs straight to Christ and the nations.

questions: Isaac clung to his favorite son even against God's revealed word. Where might a personal preference be blinding you to what God has actually said?
Rebekah and Jacob believed the promise but grasped for it through deceit. Where are you tempted to force a good outcome by wrong means instead of trusting God to keep His word?
Esau wept for a blessing he had earlier despised. Is there something of God's that you treated lightly and now feel the loss of?
The whole family is fractured by favoritism and lies. How have favoritism or dishonesty wounded a family you know, and what would honesty and trust look like instead?
God kept His promise despite this family's mess. How does it comfort you that God's purposes are not finally dependent on your performance?

translationNotes.note: Esau's line 'Is he not rightly named Jacob' plays on the name Jacob, which sounds like the Hebrew for he grasps the heel or he deceives; the pun ties his name to his character.
The phrase rendered 'away from the richness of the land' can also be read 'of the richness of the land,' and translators differ; the surrounding lines make clear Esau's portion is the harder one.
